title: Protein Quality Control and Organelle Turnover

generated.pipeline: extract -> Codex draft -> Codex accuracy gate and fix

cards.front: For a defined cellular pool over a defined interval, change equals {{c1::arrival minus clearance}}.
cards.back: A pool grows when arrival exceeds clearance and shrinks when clearance exceeds arrival.
cards.quote: For a defined cellular pool over a defined interval, its change equals arrival minus clearance.

cards.front: Why can a high cellular pool measured at one time not reveal its flux?
cards.back: The pool could be high because arrival increased or because clearance slowed; one snapshot does not distinguish those rates.
cards.quote: A high level measured at one time therefore cannot tell whether arrival increased or clearance slowed.

cards.front: How can temporarily blocking a clearance route estimate flux through that route?
cards.back: Measure the extra accumulation during a complete block, provided the block does not change arrival during the interval.
cards.quote: Temporarily blocking a clearance route and measuring the additional accumulation can estimate flux through that route

cards.front: The 26S proteasome's protein-degrading active sites face inward in its hollow {{c1::20S core}}.
cards.back: Regulatory caps control access to the core.
cards.quote: The 26S proteasome, found in the cytosol and nucleus, has a hollow 20S core whose active sites face inward.
cards.section: Physical constraints on the two exits

cards.front: How does the 26S proteasome prepare a ubiquitinated protein for degradation?
cards.back: Its caps recognize ubiquitin chains, remove ubiquitin for reuse, and use ATP to unfold and thread the protein into the core.
cards.quote: Its regulatory caps recognise ubiquitin chains, remove ubiquitin for reuse, and use ATP to unfold and thread an engaged protein into the core.
cards.section: Physical constraints on the two exits

cards.front: A lysosomal {{c1::V-ATPase}} uses ATP to acidify the lumen so hydrolases work well.
cards.back: It is an ATP-powered proton pump.
cards.quote: In a lysosome, a V-ATPase—an ATP-powered proton pump—acidifies the lumen so digestive enzymes called hydrolases work well
cards.section: Physical constraints on the two exits

cards.front: How does macroautophagy deliver cytoplasmic material to lysosomal hydrolases?
cards.back: A cup-shaped membrane encloses cytoplasm as a double-membrane autophagosome, which fuses with a lysosome for digestion.
cards.quote: The autophagosome fuses with a lysosome, and the inner membrane and its contents are digested; the building blocks return to the cytosol.
cards.section: Physical constraints on the two exits

cards.front: LC3 attached to phosphatidylethanolamine is the lipid-linked form called {{c1::LC3-II}}.
cards.back: LC3-II coats autophagosome membranes.
cards.quote: this lipid-linked LC3-II coats autophagosome membranes, and inner-membrane copies are destroyed in the lysosome.
cards.section: Physical constraints on the two exits

cards.front: A cell must dispose of one unfolded protein and one intact damaged organelle. Which route is physically suited to each, and why?
cards.back: The proteasome can unfold and thread the individual protein through its narrow core. A lysosomal autophagy route can engulf the intact organelle as bulk cargo. This follows from how each route admits cargo.
cards.quote: The proteasome cannot admit an intact organelle or large aggregate through its narrow pore; an individual substrate must be engaged and unfolded.
cards.section: Route overlap and flux limits

cards.front: Assume bafilomycin completely blocks clearance, LC3-II accumulation is linear, and carrier formation is unchanged. LC3-II is 1.0 without and 2.0 with bafilomycin in control cells; 1.5 without and 4.5 with it in starved cells; and 3.0 without and 3.2 with it after Drug D. Calculate each flux over the interval.
cards.back: Flux = with inhibitor − without inhibitor. Control: 2.0 − 1.0 = 1.0. Starved: 4.5 − 1.5 = 3.0. Drug D: 3.2 − 3.0 = 0.2.
cards.quote: flux over the interval = LC3-II with bafilomycin − LC3-II without bafilomycin
cards.section: Read a flow, not a still picture

cards.front: Assume LC3-II accumulation is linear and bafilomycin does not change carrier formation. Drug D produces high LC3-II without bafilomycin but adds only 0.2 more with saturating bafilomycin. What happens and why?
cards.back: LC3-II accumulates while flux is low. The pattern points to blocked fusion or degradation, not increased induction, because inhibiting lysosomal clearance adds little further LC3-II.
cards.quote: Its pattern points to a block at fusion or degradation, not induction; these lanes cannot say which step fails.
cards.section: Read a flow, not a still picture

cards.front: Why should p62 be measured alongside LC3-II when interpreting autophagic flux?
cards.back: LC3-II marks the carrier, whereas p62 is destroyed with cargo. Together they test whether carrier behavior reflects cargo degradation, though p62 production can also change.
cards.quote: LC3-II marks the carrier, not its cargo, so confirm the interpretation with cargo.
cards.section: Read a flow, not a still picture

cards.front: A tandem red-and-green LC3 reporter is used. What fluorescence is expected after normal lysosomal delivery versus a block before fusion, and why?
cards.back: Normal delivery gives red-only dots because lysosomal acidity quenches green. A pre-fusion block leaves red-and-green dots outside the acidic lysosome.
cards.quote: lysosomal acidity quenches green fluorescence, so normal delivery gives red-only dots, while a block before fusion leaves red-and-green dots.
cards.section: Read a flow, not a still picture

cards.front: Design the inhibitor portion of an LC3-II turnover assay so that the difference between lanes estimates flux validly.
cards.back: Use a saturating inhibitor briefly enough to keep accumulation linear and limit secondary effects. Verify that carrier formation remains unchanged; otherwise the with-minus-without difference mixes arrival with clearance.
cards.quote: use the inhibitor at a saturating dose for a short enough time that accumulation stays in its linear range
cards.section: Read a flow, not a still picture

cards.front: A lysosomal inhibitor also increases autophagosome formation during an LC3-II assay. What happens to the usual flux estimate and why?
cards.back: The estimate becomes invalid because extra LC3-II accumulation now reflects both changed arrival and blocked clearance, violating the unchanged-formation assumption.
cards.quote: That would break the worked problem's assumption that arrival remains unchanged during the block.
cards.section: Route overlap and flux limits

cards.front: What does BiP bind on a newly entering ER protein?
cards.back: BiP binds exposed hydrophobic stretches and helps the protein fold.
cards.quote: BiP, an Hsp70-family chaperone, binds exposed hydrophobic stretches and helps it fold.
cards.section: The ER: retry, remove, raise capacity

cards.front: How do calnexin and calreticulin retain an incompletely folded glycoprotein for another folding attempt?
cards.back: They bind its N-linked glycan when one terminal glucose remains; calnexin is membrane-bound and calreticulin is soluble.
cards.quote: When one remains, the lectin chaperones calnexin, which is membrane-bound, and calreticulin, which is soluble, bind that sugar
cards.section: The ER: retry, remove, raise capacity

cards.front: A glycoprotein released from calnexin still has non-native features. What happens next and why?
cards.back: UGGT adds one glucose back, allowing another round with calnexin or calreticulin. Reglucosylation is a retry ticket, not a disposal label.
cards.quote: UGGT recognizes features of a still-non-native client and adds one glucose back.
cards.section: The ER: retry, remove, raise capacity

cards.front: Movement of a failed protein back across the ER membrane is called {{c1::retrotranslocation}}.
cards.back: This moves an ERAD client toward the cytosolic proteasome.
cards.quote: Moving back across the ER membrane is called retrotranslocation.
cards.section: The ER: retry, remove, raise capacity

cards.front: Trace a failed glycoprotein from ER retention through ER-associated degradation.
cards.back: Mannose trimming helps mark it; it is retrotranslocated, ubiquitinated by an ER E3 ligase, extracted by Cdc48/p97, and passed to the proteasome.
cards.quote: The ATP-powered extraction machine Cdc48—p97 or VCP in mammals—pulls the client out and passes it to the proteasome.
cards.section: The ER: retry, remove, raise capacity

cards.front: An ERAD substrate accumulates. Its immunoprecipitate either lacks ubiquitin or contains abundant ubiquitin while the substrate remains membrane-bound. What does each result suggest?
cards.back: No ubiquitin suggests a defect at or before E3 tagging. Ubiquitinated substrate stuck in membranes suggests a later extraction defect such as loss of Cdc48 function.
cards.quote: ubiquitinated substrate stuck in membranes suggests a later step, such as extraction by Cdc48.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: After synthesis is stopped, an ERAD substrate has a 20-minute half-life. What fraction and percentage remain after 60 minutes?
cards.back: 60/20 = 3 half-lives. Remaining fraction = (1/2)^3 = 1/8 = 0.125, so 12.5% remains.
cards.quote: Three half-lives leave one eighth, or 12.5%, in wild type.
cards.section: The ER: retry, remove, raise capacity

cards.front: How does the unfolded protein response address excess failed proteins in the ER?
cards.back: It raises folding and disposal capacity; mammalian PERK also reduces the incoming protein load. Prolonged unresolved stress can drive cell death.
cards.quote: It raises folding and disposal machinery and, through PERK in mammals, slows the incoming load of new proteins.
cards.section: The ER: retry, remove, raise capacity

cards.front: In budding yeast, Ire1 cuts an intron from {{c1::HAC1 mRNA}} so the Hac1 transcription factor can be made.
cards.back: Budding yeast has one UPR branch.
cards.quote: Budding yeast has one branch: the sensor Ire1 cuts an intron from HAC1 mRNA so the Hac1 transcription factor can be made.
cards.section: The ER: retry, remove, raise capacity

cards.front: What are the immediate outputs of the three mammalian UPR sensors IRE1, PERK, and ATF6?
cards.back: IRE1 splices XBP1 mRNA; PERK phosphorylates eIF2α; ATF6 is cleaved in the Golgi to release a transcription factor.
cards.quote: Mammals have three overlapping branches: IRE1 removes a 26-nucleotide intron from XBP1 mRNA
cards.section: The ER: retry, remove, raise capacity

cards.front: PERK phosphorylates eIF2α during ER stress. What happens to translation and the ER protein load, and why?
cards.back: Most translation slows, reducing new proteins entering the ER, while ATF4 is translated preferentially.
cards.quote: PERK phosphorylates eIF2α on serine 51, slowing most translation while permitting preferential translation of ATF4
cards.section: The ER: retry, remove, raise capacity

cards.front: Tunicamycin-treated mouse fibroblasts lacking IRE1α still cleave ATF6 and induce BiP mRNA. What does this establish about mammalian UPR organization?
cards.back: The branches operate in parallel and remain experimentally separable: loss of IRE1α does not silence ATF6 processing or all stress-induced transcription.
cards.quote: One broken branch does not silence the response.
cards.section: UPR discovery and branch overlap

cards.front: Selective autophagy of mitochondria is called {{c1::mitophagy}}.
cards.back: Selective-autophagy receptors link chosen cargo to the LC3 family.
cards.quote: Mitophagy is selective autophagy of mitochondria.
cards.section: Selective autophagy: choosing a mitochondrion

cards.front: How does loss of mitochondrial membrane potential initiate the PINK1–Parkin mitophagy route in cultured cells?
cards.back: PINK1 accumulates on depolarized mitochondria and recruits Parkin, which ubiquitinates outer-membrane proteins so receptors recruit autophagy machinery.
cards.quote: Parkin adds ubiquitin to outer-membrane proteins, and ubiquitin-binding receptors recruit the autophagy machinery that engulfs the mitochondrion.
cards.section: Selective autophagy: choosing a mitochondrion

cards.front: Atg5-null fibroblasts still recruit Parkin to depolarized mitochondria, but the mitochondria remain. Which step changes and why?
cards.back: Mitochondrial clearance fails, but Parkin recruitment does not. Atg5 acts in conventional autophagosome building downstream of mitochondrial tagging.
cards.quote: Clearance needs Atg5, but recruitment does not.
cards.section: Selective autophagy: choosing a mitochondrion

cards.front: Why does Parkin recruitment alone not demonstrate completion of mitophagy?
cards.back: Recruitment shows tagging, an upstream event. Tagged mitochondria can remain if downstream autophagosome building or clearance fails.
cards.quote: The mitochondria remain, so a tag alone does not remove the cargo.
cards.section: Selective autophagy: choosing a mitochondrion

cards.front: A whole-animal tissue retains basal mitophagy after Pink1 loss. Does that refute the cultured-cell PINK1–Parkin mechanism? Explain.
cards.back: No. The cultured-cell results establish one route under the tested depolarization conditions, not the only route in an animal. Preserved basal mitophagy implies other routes can operate.
cards.quote: PINK1 and Parkin are a well-proven route for damaged mitochondria in cultured cells, not the only route in an animal.
cards.section: Selective autophagy: choosing a mitochondrion

cards.front: Design a minimal experiment set to distinguish an ERAD defect from a yeast UPR defect in cells accumulating a misfolded ER membrane protein.
cards.back: Use a cycloheximide chase to measure destruction and induce stress while measuring HAC1 splicing. Stable substrate with normal splicing favors ERAD; stress-dependent buildup with absent splicing favors UPR failure.
cards.quote: Design experiments that tell the two apart, and write down what each model predicts before you run them.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: A yeast ERAD substrate is stable in a cycloheximide chase, but tunicamycin still triggers normal HAC1 splicing. Which model is favored and why?
cards.back: An ERAD block is favored. Destruction is slow, whereas normal HAC1 splicing shows that the Ire1 step of UPR signaling still works.
cards.quote: The pair of results is stronger than either alone.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Why can a cycloheximide chase alone fail to distinguish an ERAD mutation from a UPR mutation?
cards.back: Both can slow substrate loss because yeast require an intact UPR for efficient ERAD. A UPR readout such as HAC1 splicing is needed to separate them.
cards.quote: The chase alone cannot settle it: yeast need an intact UPR for efficient ERAD
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: A plasmid carrying HRD1 rescues substrate degradation in a mutant yeast strain. What follow-up would show that the HRD1 mutation, rather than a second mutation or suppression, caused the phenotype?
cards.back: Sequence the mutant allele or remake the mutation in a clean strain and retest. Rescue alone is insufficient because an extra gene copy can suppress a different defect.
cards.quote: Rescue alone is not proof, because extra copies of one gene can suppress a defect in another
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Selective digestion of parts of the endoplasmic reticulum is called {{c1::ER-phagy}}.
cards.back: ER-phagy uses several receptors.
cards.quote: ER-phagy, the selective digestion of parts of the ER, uses several receptors.
cards.section: ER-phagy receptors

cards.front: What did the purified yeast Hrd1 reconstitution suggest about retrotranslocation?
cards.back: Hrd1 self-ubiquitination triggered substrate movement across the membrane, suggesting a ubiquitin-gated Hrd1 channel with Cdc48 completing extraction.
cards.quote: Hrd1 ubiquitinating itself triggered movement of the substrate across the membrane
cards.section: The Hrd1 channel: reconstitution and structure

cards.front: Why should the Hrd1 reconstitution not be treated as a universal mechanism for every ERAD substrate?
cards.back: It used purified yeast proteins and one membrane-anchored substrate; whether every substrate in every cell crosses this way remains unsettled.
cards.quote: Whether every ERAD substrate in every cell crosses this way is not settled.
cards.section: The Hrd1 channel: reconstitution and structure

cards.front: Mitochondrial profile density is 0.62 per µm² without YFP-Parkin and 0.074 per µm² with it. Calculate the percentage reduction and state what the result is not.
cards.back: Reduction = (0.62 − 0.074)/0.62 = 0.546/0.62 = 0.881, or 88.1% lower. It compares densities at one time; it is not a rate.
cards.quote: That compares mean two-dimensional densities in two groups of cells at one time. It is not a rate.
cards.section: Counting mitochondria after Parkin
